title: Textile factory workers in India are teaching AI how to do their jobs
key_facts: NPR's Diaa Hadid reports from Karur, southern India, where textile workers wear GoPro cameras to record their hand movements
The footage is used to train AI robots to do their jobs; developers need millions of hours of it
Worker Shobha Kiribakaran, 40, earns $90 a month and says nobody told her the recording trains AI robots
Some workers are paid to hand over the data, but many are simply ordered to
Astha Kapoor, co-founder of the Aapti Institute, called it "exploitation of labor"
Economist Amit Basole said India's government is not equipped for AI replacing workers; India has about 600 million workers
Kapoor said robots are unlikely to be deployed at scale in India soon because they are expensive to run
Worker Kannagi Periyasaamy was told she is teaching a robot and expects to be replaced; a viral video in April brought the practice to public attention
Objectways, a data firm, trains robots using head cameras and claw tools in Karur
quote_evidence: Some workers are paid to hand over this data, but many others, like Kiribakaran, are just being ordered to do it.
We can just call it what it is, which is exploitation of labor.
why_it_matters_hint: Workers are generating the training data for machines that may replace them, often without being told.
